candidates.name: LegDefinition
candidates.quote: The term leg is very general and simply means that the direction of movement has changed, using any criterion that you choose to determine that the change exists.
candidates.description: Primitive: a 'leg' is a run of price movement in one direction that ends when a direction-change criterion fires (e.g., a swing pivot, a minimum retracement, or a trend-line break). Brooks explicitly leaves the criterion open, so every other candidate in this chapter depends on picking one.

candidates.name: TwoLeggedPullbackComplete
candidates.quote: The market regularly tries to do something twice, and this is why all moves tend to subdivide into two smaller moves. This is true of both with-trend and countertrend moves.
candidates.description: A pullback against the trend has completed exactly two legs (a countertrend leg, a small with-trend leg that stays inside the trend's extreme, and a second countertrend leg) -- once the second leg is in place, the pullback is likely done and a with-trend entry is favored.

candidates.book_order_type: stop entry one tick beyond the signal bar that ends leg 2, mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open

complexity.reason: requires swing-pivot/leg detection (per T20-01) plus counting and comparing successive legs' extremes

notes: This is the chapter's central, most-mechanizable idea; expect it to be the main candidate that survives dedup from this file.

candidates.name: ABCPullbackPattern
candidates.quote: There is a countertrend move, a small with-trend move that usually does not go beyond the trend's extreme, and then a second countertrend move that usually extends deeper than the first.
candidates.description: The classic three-step ABC pullback: leg A countertrend, leg B a small with-trend bounce that fails to exceed the trend's prior extreme, leg C a second countertrend move that goes deeper than leg A -- entry with the trend once leg C completes.

candidates.book_order_type: stop entry one tick beyond the signal bar ending leg C, mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open

complexity.reason: same leg-detection dependency as T20-02, plus an added constraint on leg B's extreme relative to the prior trend extreme

notes: A more specific, three-leg-with-constraints variant of T20-02; 'composite' since it names three distinct legs (composes T20-01 three times conceptually, listed once).

candidates.name: SecondLegExceedsFirstLegExtreme
candidates.quote: other bears who shorted the first up leg will add to their shorts as soon as the second leg up goes above the high of the first leg up.
candidates.description: In a two-legged countertrend move within a trend, once leg 2 trades beyond leg 1's extreme (e.g., a rally's leg 2 high exceeds leg 1's high within a bear trend), traders who faded leg 1 add to their positions with the trend -- a breakout of leg 1's extreme by leg 2.
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry one tick beyond leg 1's extreme, mechanized as close-and-next-open once that level is taken out intrabar

complexity.reason: the comparison itself is trivial once leg 1 and leg 2 are identified, but identifying them requires the leg/pivot detection from T20-01

candidates.description: A break of the current trend line marks the start of a new leg against the trend -- the first leg of a potential two-legged pullback or reversal.

candidates.name: SecondPushFailsAtPriorExtreme
candidates.quote: When there is a clear double top or double bottom, the second push is the test of the prior price where the market reversed earlier, and if it fails again at that price, a reversal or pullback is likely.
candidates.description: A second push (leg 2) tests the extreme set by an earlier leg and fails to exceed it by more than a small tolerance -- a double top/bottom test that signals a reversal or pullback is likely.
candidates.pseudocode: fabs(leg2.extreme - leg1.extreme) <= failTolerance && leg2 reverses (close[0] crosses back through leg2's own recent extreme)
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry one tick beyond the signal bar that confirms the failure, mechanized as close-and-next-open

complexity.reason: requires leg/pivot detection (T20-01) to identify leg1 and leg2 extremes before the tolerance comparison

notes: Brooks notes real moves are often ambiguous between a two-push and a three-push pattern; this candidate only captures the double-top/bottom failure test, not the three-push variant.

chapter_summary: A short, largely conceptual chapter arguing that market moves (pullbacks, breakouts, reversals, and trends themselves) tend to subdivide into two legs, with a nod to Elliott Wave and three-push patterns as related but overlapping ideas. Almost everything here rests on an undefined 'leg' concept (T20-01, research-grade, since Brooks explicitly says the direction-change criterion is the trader's choice); every other candidate (two-legged pullback completion, the ABC pullback, a second leg exceeding the first leg's extreme, trend-line breaks starting new legs, and the double-top/bottom second-push failure test) is graded hard because it inherits that same swing/leg-detection dependency. This file supplies the fuller, more explicit leg-counting primitives that chapter 19's T19-21 (TwoLeggedPullbackRepeats) only gestured at; expect the dedup pass to merge them.
